title: Why You'd Never Want To Meet A Sperm Whale
transcript_source: YouTube auto-subs (en), deduplicated rolling captions; ~1,674 words recovered (a few line ends dropped by auto-sub)

chapters.title: What a sperm whale really eats
The Essex: the whale that fought back

title_pattern.template: Why You'd Never Want To Meet A [Creature]
title_pattern.notes: Second-person, negative-framing curiosity title ('never want to'), implies personal danger without stating a fact. Pure creature name as the object, no numbers. Works as a series format (swap creature). Paired thumbnail text adds a NEW claim ('IT HEARS YOU..') instead of repeating the title.

thumbnail.composition: 16:9, pure black background. Huge sperm-whale head enters from the right and fills ~60% of the frame (head-on 3/4 view, open lower jaw with a row of teeth at bottom). Tiny scuba diver with a torch beam lower-left (~3% of frame height). Concentric sonar arcs radiate from the whale's snout toward the diver. A hand-drawn red curved arrow runs from the text down to the diver.
thumbnail.text: "IT HEARS YOU.." top-left, heavy condensed sans in caps; 'IT HEARS' white, 'YOU..' red. Double-dot ellipsis.
thumbnail.colours: Monochrome black/white/grey scratchboard (engraved etching) illustration + a single accent red (text word + arrow). Very high contrast.
thumbnail.subject_scale_contrast: Extreme: giant scarred whale head vs a speck-sized human. The arrow is needed to find the diver, which forces the viewer to 'discover' the victim.
thumbnail.style_note: Thumbnail is a detailed etching-style illustration, completely different from the flat vector style inside the video (bait-and-switch in rendering quality, not content).
thumbnail.why_it_works: One clear threat story readable in <1 s: monster + tiny you + the invisible weapon (sound arcs). 'YOU' in red makes it personal; the arrow points at the viewer-surrogate. Black background pops against YouTube's white/dark UI. Text adds a hook not in the title (sound/hearing) so title+thumb together form a question.

hook.verbatim_0_5s: Picture this. You're floating in the open ocean and you've done your homework.
hook.verbatim_0_28s: Picture this. You're floating in the open ocean and you've done your homework. Sharks are rare out here. Orcas tend to leave divers alone. Nothing in the sea is actually looking for you. That's the rule. Then you feel it. Not see it, feel it. A deep knocking in your chest like someone tapping on your ribs from the inside. That's a sperm whale and it already knows exactly where you are.
hook.device: Second-person 'Picture this' immersion + false-safety checklist (each item ticked with a green check: SHARKS: RARE, ORCAS: LEAVE DIVERS ALONE, NOTHING IS HUNTING YOU) then rule-break ('Then you feel it'). Sensory detail (knocking in your chest) replaces a visual reveal. Open loop paid off at 3:45 ('Remember that knocking from the start? That was you being scanned') and bookended at 9:29 ('We tell ourselves nothing in the sea is really looking for us').
hook.visual: Flat vector scuba diver gliding across a deep-blue gradient ocean with god-rays and drifting particles; small UI-style captions with check icons appear lower-left; slow push-in to the diver's chest with a pulsing ring; real stock clip of a whale+diver at 0:24; sonar rings hit the diver inside red targeting brackets with red text IT KNOWS WHERE YOU ARE.

beats.summary: Second-person scenario: you're diving, safety checklist ticked off, then a knocking in your chest - a sperm whale already knows where you are.
Not orcas or breaching humpbacks: the sperm whale is 'a different category' - biggest toothed predator ever, hunts where no mammal can, sank a ship on purpose (three-item stacked claim list).
'So let's talk about why you'd never want to be in the water with one.'
~16 m, ~40 t = city bus / 6-7 elephants; head is a third of the body; narrow lower jaw; hand-sized 1 kg teeth on bottom jaw only; contrast with filter-feeding humpback - 'It grabs.'
Question card 'What does it eat?' -> 'Squid.' Giant/colossal squid with hooks and beaks; scars as proof; stomachs with thousands of undigested beaks - 'a receipt for every meal' joke.
Dives 2 km+, holds breath over an hour vs you struggling for 1 minute in a pool; light disappears with depth -> 'So how does it find anything?'

Sound: head = biological speaker, spermaceti organ focuses clicks into a beam ('flashlight made of sound'); echoes form a picture; loudest animal on Earth ~236 dB; divers feel clicks in their chest - callback: 'That was you being scanned.'
1980s theory that clicks could stun prey - never proven, but scientists seriously considering it shows how loud it is.

Largest brain ever (~8 kg, heavier than a bowling ball); codas; 2024 Dominica study of ~9,000 codas found alphabet-like structure and clan dialects; re-immersion 'picture it again' + joke 'I'd like to know what it said... actually no.'

'Has it ever turned on people? Yes, once, very famously.' Essex 1820 rammed twice, crew adrift, inspired Moby-Dick; Ann Alexander 1851; battering-ram hypothesis; twist of sympathy - 'that wasn't an attack, it was a complaint.'
'What would you actually do?' Four numbered options (swim away, dive and hide, stay still, scare it off), each knocked down with a punchline and struck through; verdict: nothing you could do.
But they almost never come after people: no pattern of hunting humans, calm curiosity with permitted swimmers in Dominica, 'you vs a fly' analogy; eerie vertical sleeping naps.

beats.beat_type: moral turn: humans are the danger
beats.summary: Danger goes the other way: centuries of whaling, ~1.1M -> about a third left, 25,000/yr in the 1960s, 1980s moratorium; modern threats (ship strikes, fishing gear, noise, plastic); longline stealing - callback to colossal squid 'caught stealing someone's dinner'.
Iron-rich waste feeds plankton that pull carbon; Southern Ocean sperm whales remove ~240,000 t carbon/yr - 'gardening the ocean'.
Callback to opening rule: nothing in the sea is looking for us - but 2 km down something with the biggest brain is listening, talking, remembering. 'It just has better things to do than us.'
Thanks for watching, comment which deep-sea creature next ('I do actually read them'), watch-next end-screen box.

pacing.notes: Narration is brisk and conversational (~170 wpm, short sentences, frequent jokes). Hard scene cuts every ~7 s on average, but within each scene a new element/caption/counter is added roughly every 2-4 s, so the screen never sits still. Each 2 s contact-sheet sample differs visibly from the previous one ~85% of the time. Stock footage is <5% of runtime (about 6 short clips: 0:23, 0:35-0:40, 2:14, 8:30); everything else is flat 2D vector animation. Chapter lengths 50-125 s; open loops roughly every 60-90 s ('so how does it...', 'has it ever...', 'what would you do?').

style_system.palette: Deep navy/teal underwater gradient (#0b1a26 -> #164a66) with vertical light shafts and drifting bokeh particles; whales in warm grey; text white; accent red (#e53935-ish) for danger words/underlines/stamps; accent green for checkmarks and sonar HUD; warm beige sky for surface/history scenes; sepia for 1800s; bright pool blue for 'you' comparisons.
style_system.typography: Small, wide, bold geometric/grotesk all-caps labels (letter-spaced), usually top-centre or lower-left, sometimes inside dark rounded pills; key words in red with red underline; occasional big centred one-word cards ('SQUID.', 'SOUND.', 'YES.').
style_system.characters: Reusable flat-vector assets: scuba diver (side and top-down), sperm whale side profile (with jaw/teeth variants, silhouette variant, vertical sleeping variant), squid, ships, stick figures for 'you'/scientists.
style_system.recurring_devices: Rubber-stamp slams (CANCEL, COMPLAINT, STOPPED, WINNER, MONSTER); counters that tick up; progress/meter bars; numbered option menus with strike-through; paper documents sliding in; split-screen comparisons; green sonar/x-ray HUD.

techniques_worth_copying: Second-person cold open with a ticked 'safety checklist' that the twist breaks; plant a sensory detail (knocking in chest) and pay it off 3 minutes later with a callback ('That was you being scanned').
Bookend structure: final line rephrases the opening 'rule' (nothing in the sea is looking for you) with a twist.
Relatable unit conversions in visuals: city bus, 6-7 elephants, hand-sized tooth, bowling-ball brain, you holding breath in a pool for 0:15.
Question cards as chapter transitions: 'WHAT DOES IT EAT?' -> 'SQUID.'; 'NO LIGHT. SO HOW DOES IT HUNT?' -> 'SOUND.'; 'AGAINST PEOPLE?' -> 'YES.'
Game-like options menu ('YOUR OPTIONS 1-4') where each option is knocked out with a joke and struck through, ending on a red verdict line - turns facts into interactive survival scenario.
Rubber-stamp gags and paper props (receipt, official complaint, moratorium document) as comic punctuation every 1-2 minutes.
Animated counters and meters for every number (dB bar, depth counter, beak counter, population isotype grid, carbon tonnes) - numbers are never just spoken.
Moral reversal in the last third: the 'monster' is the victim (arrow flips direction), then an unexpected positive fact (ocean gardener) for an uplifting close - drives comments.
Consistent minimal asset library reused across scenes; a few seconds of stock footage only as 'proof it's real' punctuation.
Thumbnail uses a much more detailed illustration style than the video, with one accent colour and a red arrow to a tiny human for scale contrast.
Chapters with curiosity titles in the description plus an engagement CTA ('which creature next? I do actually read them').

code_only_remake_needs.feasibility: Very high - ~95% of the video is flat 2D vector motion graphics that map directly to Remotion + SVG. Stock clips can be replaced by more vector scenes or a stylised 'proof' card.
assets: SVG creature library: side-profile whale with separate jaw/teeth/eye layers, silhouette and vertical variants; squid with animatable tentacles; scuba diver side and top-down with fin-kick loop; stick figure; ships (sailing, steam whaler, lifeboats); elephants, bus, hand, bowling ball, brain, receipt, wallet, book cover, document sheets, kitchen lamp, fly

Background components: underwater vertical gradient with animated god-ray shafts and drifting particle bokeh; depth-dependent colour ramp (light to black) driven by a depth prop; surface/sky split scene; sepia parchment; pool lanes

Text components: letter-spaced caps label, dark rounded caption pill, red underlined emphasis, big centred one-word card, check-icon chip, stacked bullet list, numbered option menu with highlight box and animated strike-through
motion_components: Sonar/ripple rings (concentric expanding stroke circles) and a sound-beam cone
Green HUD layer: sonar sweep, x-ray body outline with glowing lungs, targeting corner brackets
Number counter (interpolate + toLocaleString), horizontal gradient meter, vertical VU meters, circular timer ring, depth ruler that scrolls
Isotype grid (N icons, fade subset), pie chart draw-on, block grid that fills, balance scale tip
Rubber stamp slam (scale 1.6->1 with rotation, slight camera shake), document slide-in, receipt scroll
Camera: slow push-in/zoom on a scene group, vertical descent pan, impact shake; ink-blot wipe and fade-to-black transitions
code_only_remake_needs.audio: Local TTS (Kokoro) narration at ~165-170 wpm with conversational punctuation; low ambient underwater drone bed; click/thump SFX for sonar and stamps (generated or CC0).
code_only_remake_needs.pipeline: Script -> beat list with on-screen text and a 'visual verb' per 2-4 s (add counter, slam stamp, push-in) -> storyboard JSON scenes referencing reusable components -> TTS + word timestamps for syncing label pops -> Remotion render 1920x1080 30fps.
code_only_remake_needs.thumbnail: Separate high-detail illustration is the hardest part to do in code; approximate with a large layered SVG/canvas head rendered with noise/hatching filters (feTurbulence + displacement, stroked line hatching) on black, tiny diver, red text + hand-drawn red arrow path.
